candidate_sources.title: Caliciopsis Canker (pine canker) Caliciopsis pinea
candidate_sources.snippet: Caliciopsis pinea is found on eastern and western white pine, and at least some firs. It is a perennial fungus producing small ascocarps throughout the spring and summer, with ascospores being rain-splash disseminated or dispersed by insects and small mammals. The most conspicuous symptom of infection is streaming resin (resinosis) on the trunk and branches, and signs include small, curved, black-colored stalks or 'eyelashes.'

candidate_sources.title: A Diagnostic Guide for Caliciopsis Canker Disease on North American Conifers | Plant Health Progress
candidate_sources.snippet: Caliciopsis canker disease (CCD) is caused by multiple Caliciopsis species infecting various North American conifers, with Caliciopsis pinea on eastern and western white pines being the most extensively characterized. Branch and trunk cankers appear smooth, depressed and reddish-brown; signs include small black spore-bearing stalks ('eyelashes'). Severity is influenced by environmental stressors such as drought and stand density.

candidate_sources.title: Extent and Severity of Caliciopsis Canker in New England, USA: An Emerging Disease of Eastern White Pine (Pinus strobus L.)
candidate_sources.snippet: Caliciopsis pinea is a stem canker pathogen posing a significant threat to white pine health in the northeastern US. External symptoms include profuse pitching from small, round or elongated cankers in the mid to upper bole, sunken resinous cankers, bark cracking, and crown thinning. The disease is associated with overstocked stands and poor sites; pole-sized and suppressed trees are more likely to be damaged than dominant trees.

candidate_sources.title: Canavirgella Needlecast of Pine â€” New Needlecast Disease for Connecticut | The Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (CAES)
candidate_sources.snippet: When needles are infected with Canavirgella, the bases of the symptomatic needles usually remain green and the needles and the fascicle often remain attached to the tree. The pathogen commonly causes the tips of the current year's needles to die in early summer and turn tan, and finally reddish-brown by early fall. Lophophacidium dooksii (formerly Canavirgella banfieldii) is the fungus responsible for this disease of Eastern white pine. Infection of succulent, elongating, current-season needles occurs in late June or early July; extended periods with free water on the needles are conducive for infection. Controlled by good sanitary and cultural practices.

candidate_sources.title: White Pine Needlecast â€” Insect & Disease Fact Sheets | Maine Forest Service, Maine DACF
candidate_sources.snippet: White Pine Needlecast fact sheet from the Maine Forest Service Forest Health & Monitoring program, describing the needle cast complex affecting eastern white pine (Pinus strobus), symptoms of needle browning and premature needle drop, the responsible foliar fungi, and management considerations.

candidate_sources.title: Canavirgella Needlecast of White Pine | University of New Hampshire Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: UNH Cooperative Extension fact sheet on Canavirgella needlecast of white pine, caused by Canavirgella banfieldii (Lophophacidium dooksii). Tips of current-year needles die in early summer, turning tan then reddish-brown by fall while needle bases remain green. Covers symptoms, disease cycle, infection conditions, and cultural management on eastern white pine.

candidate_sources.title: Eastern White Pine â€” Threats to a Historically Important Species | Penn State Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: In white pine there are several potential needle cast diseases, with the most pathogenic in the eastern US being Bifusella linearis and Canavirgella banfieldii. B. linearis and C. banfieldii cause tips of current-year needles to die in early summer, turning tan then reddish-brown by early fall; many species of Lophodermium are also reported as needle cast fungi. Increased Mayâ€“July precipitation during needle elongation correlates with greater needle disease damage.

candidate_sources.title: Red Ring Rot of Eastern White Pine caused by Porodaedalea | UMass Amherst CAFE
candidate_sources.snippet: Red ring rot of conifers is caused by the fungal pathogen Porodaedalea, and focuses on red ring rot of eastern white pine (Pinus strobus). Red ring rot results in a selective delignification (white rot) of infected wood tissue. Small, elliptical decay pockets are lined with white cellulose fibers. Affected heartwood takes on a reddish purple hue, developing into spindle-shaped pockets of black-flecked white rot surrounded by sound, reddish wood. Signs include shelf-shaped conks protruding from trunks.

candidate_sources.title: Red Ring Rot | Forest Pathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Red ring rot (Porodaedalea pini, formerly Phellinus pini) is one of the most important stem decays of conifers. Spores enter trees through branch stubs in the mid to upper trunk and decay the heartwood, producing characteristic white pocket rot. Conks (punk knots) form at branch stubs.

candidate_sources.title: FOR356/FR425: Red Heart Disease in Pines caused by Porodaedalea (Phellinus) pini in Florida | UF/IFAS
candidate_sources.snippet: Red heart disease (red ring rot) in pines is caused by Porodaedalea (Phellinus) pini. The fungus causes a white rot of heartwood, entering through branch stubs and wounds, with conks forming on the trunk. Describes symptoms, pathogen biology, and management.

candidate_sources.title: Eastern White Pine (Pinus strobus) Diseases | University of Kentucky Plant Pathology
candidate_sources.snippet: Eastern white pine (Pinus strobus) is a popular conifer. Red-rot disease, also known as pencil rot and red-ring rot, is caused by the fungus Porodaedalea pini (formerly Phellinus pini). The fungus may produce conks on live trees and 'punk knots' at branch stubs. Windborne spores infect wounds from logging or broken branches.

candidate_sources.title: White pine blister rust | UMN Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: White pine blister rust is caused by the exotic fungus Cronartium ribicola. The first symptom is a yellow or red spot on infected needles in spring; cankered (dead and sunken) areas form on trunks and branches with pitch flow and conspicuous yellowish-orange spores. The fungus cannot spread pine to pine but must infect a currant or gooseberry (Ribes) plant first.

candidate_sources.title: White Pine Blister Rust â€“ Wisconsin Horticulture
candidate_sources.snippet: Infection of needles by Cronartium ribicola results in yellow to brown spots and bands. A typical canker has resinous margins and may appear 'blistered' before rupturing to expose fruiting bodies with yellow to bright orange spores. Management includes pruning lower branches, removing severely infected trees, and removing currants or gooseberries within a one-mile radius.

candidate_sources.title: White Pine Blister Rust (Cronartium ribicola) - Hort Answers, University of Illinois Extension
candidate_sources.snippet: White Pine Blister Rust caused by Cronartium ribicola on white pine (Pinus strobus). Common symptoms include flagging branches, broken branches, and dying treetops (topkill), with cankers on trunks and branches. The spore that carries the disease from Ribes to pine rarely survives airborne transport beyond 900 feet.
